verses.note: God calls the sign by the name of the covenant it signifies. Christian theology uses the same way of speaking for the sacraments, as when Jesus says of the cup that it is ‘the new covenant in my blood’ (Luke 22:20), and the traditions differ on how closely sign and reality are joined.

Paul calls circumcision ‘a seal of the righteousness’ Abraham had by faith before he was circumcised (Romans 4:11). The sign confirms a promise already received; it does not create Abraham's standing with God.

Christians have long connected circumcision with baptism because Colossians 2:11-12 links the two. Those who baptize infants see in Isaac's eighth-day circumcision a covenant sign given to a child before he could believe; those who baptize believers only hold that the New Testament sign follows faith and that the link in Colossians is spiritual rather than a pattern for infants. Both positions are held by faithful churches.

The covenant sign is not treated as optional ceremony. The scene shows that a sign God appoints carries real weight, and Christian readers have often drawn from it the seriousness of the signs God gives his people, whatever their view of how those signs relate to the covenant.

The verse creates a rite whose purpose is remembrance in the full biblical sense: each generation keeps the day as participants in the rescue, not only as heirs of its story. Jesus's words at the Supper, ‘Do this in remembrance of me’, draw on this vocabulary, and Christians differ over what that remembrance involves, from a memorial of Christ's death (Zwingli and the Baptist tradition) to a real sharing in his body and blood (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Reformed traditions, each explaining the presence differently).

The rescued sufferer's feast shared with the poor became, for many Christian readers, a picture of the Lord's Supper. Augustine, in his Expositions of the Psalms, read the eating of the poor and of the rich (verse 29) in that light. The psalm itself describes the Old Testament thanksgiving meal; the link is typological.

Christians have long connected this verse with baptism. Those who hold a sacramental view (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and many Anglican and Reformed) see in baptism the sign and instrument of the cleansing Ezekiel promised. Those who hold a symbolic or ordinance view (Baptists and many free churches) see baptism as the public witness to a cleansing the Spirit has already done. Both read Ezekiel's water as God's own act of purification.

The verbs of this meal are the verbs of the Last Supper (14:22), and early Christians, reading Mark, would have heard them together; John's feeding story leads directly into the discourse on the bread of life (John 6:35-58). Interpreters differ on how far the feeding itself is meant to point to the Lord's Supper: many see a deliberate foreshadowing, while others caution that the take, bless, break, give sequence was simply the shape of every Jewish meal. Either way, Jesus is shown as the host who feeds God's people from his own hands.

The verbs of this meal are the verbs of the Lord's Supper, and the church has long read the feedings with the Eucharist in view. Christians differ on how much sacramental meaning Mark intends: some see the feedings as anticipations of the church's meal, others as signs of Jesus' provision that the Supper later takes up. The shared vocabulary is not in doubt.

The passage has been central in the debate over infant baptism, though it does not mention baptism. Calvin (Institutes 4.16.7) argued that if Christ embraced infants and declared the kingdom theirs, they should not be kept from the sign of the covenant; Oscar Cullmann (Baptism in the New Testament, 1950) noted that ‘hinder’ appears in baptismal settings (Acts 8:36, 10:47). Baptists reply that the children are blessed, not baptized, and that the kingdom belongs to all who receive it like a child, which calls for faith. Tertullian (On Baptism 18) knew the verse and still counseled delaying baptism. Christians remain divided on this second-order question.

The words of institution in Mark are the shortest of the four accounts and lack Paul's and Luke's command, ‘Do this in remembrance of me’. Churches read ‘this is my body’ as real change, real presence, spiritual presence, or memorial sign; all agree that Jesus gives himself to his followers in the act and that the church repeats it at his word.

Christians read the verse differently. Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran theology, citing it with John 3:5 and Acts 2:38, teaches that God ordinarily gives new birth through baptism received in faith. Baptist and many Reformed and evangelical Christians read baptism as the expected public confession of a faith already given, and point to the verse's own second half, which condemns unbelief alone. All sides should remember that the verse belongs to the disputed ending.

Christians differ on whether this meal is the Lord's Supper. Catholic, Orthodox, and many Anglican and Lutheran interpreters read it as eucharistic, pointing to the verbs of 22:19 and to ‘the breaking of bread’ in Acts 2:42. Many evangelical interpreters see an ordinary evening meal in which Jesus' familiar gesture gives him away. Both readings agree that Christ makes himself known at the table.

Christians read the water differently, and each reading has long standing. Most church fathers, and the Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran traditions, see a reference to baptism as the means by which the Spirit gives new birth. Calvin, in his commentary, took water and Spirit as one thing, the Spirit who cleanses like water, and many Reformed and Baptist interpreters follow him in reading Ezekiel 36 behind the verse. Ben Witherington (New Testament Studies 35, 1989) argued that water means physical birth, so that one must be born both naturally and spiritually; others see John the Baptist's baptism of repentance. The text does not settle the question by itself, and the church has not agreed on it.

Baptism in Jesus' name was administered by his disciples, not by his own hand, yet it counts as his: the report says Jesus was making and baptizing disciples. The church has drawn from this that the one who baptizes is Christ, whoever pours the water, as Augustine argued against the Donatists, who held that baptism depended on the worthiness of the minister: whether Peter or Judas baptizes, he said, it is Christ who baptizes (Tractates on John 6).

The sequence of taking, giving thanks, and giving is the pattern of every Jewish meal, and it is also the pattern of the Lord's Supper as the church remembered it. John does not say this meal was a Eucharist, but his wording lets the church's table sound in the background of a sign about bread given by Jesus' own hand.

The wording ‘the bread ... is my flesh ... for’ resembles Luke's words of institution, ‘This is My body, given for you’ (Luke 22:19). Ignatius of Antioch, early in the second century, calls the Eucharist the flesh of Jesus Christ (To the Smyrnaeans 7; To the Romans 7). Readers who find the Supper here start from this verse; readers who do not note that the future ‘I will give’ points first to the cross.

Christians read verses 53-58 in five main ways. Roman Catholics read them of the Eucharist, in which the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood (Council of Trent, Session 13, 1551; the Catechism, 1406, cites 6:51, 54, and 56). The Orthodox also read them of the Eucharist, confessing with John of Damascus (Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 4.13) that the gifts are changed by the Spirit, without defining the manner. Lutherans confess Christ's true body and blood received orally in the Supper, yet the Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration 7) reads John 6 of the spiritual eating by faith that must accompany it. The Reformed, with Calvin and the Westminster Confession (29.7), teach a real feeding on Christ by faith through the Spirit, which the Supper seals. Memorialists, including most Baptists, read the verses as a vivid picture of believing in Jesus' death, pointing to 6:35, 6:47, and 6:63. Each reading is held by faithful churches.

The verse ties baptism to forgiveness and to the Spirit, and the traditions read the tie differently: as the means through which God grants both (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran), as the appointed moment of forgiveness for a penitent believer (Stone-Campbell churches), as the sign and seal joined to what it signifies (Reformed), or as the commanded public sign of a forgiveness received by repentance and faith (Baptist and many evangelicals). The chapter note sets these out; each tradition affirms that forgiveness is God's free gift through Christ.

‘The breaking of the bread’ may mean the Lord's Supper, the common meal, or both, since in the earliest church the Supper was eaten within a meal (1 Corinthians 11:20-26). Luke used the phrase for the risen Jesus being known in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:35).

A sign and seal confirms a reality already given; it does not produce it. Reformed covenant theology, noting Colossians 2:11-12, has drawn a line from circumcision to baptism and used it to support infant baptism as a sign of the covenant; Baptist interpreters reply that the new covenant sign belongs to those who themselves believe, as Abraham believed before he received the seal. Both appeal to this verse.

This verse is one of the central texts in every tradition's account of baptism, and the positions divide over what the word ‘into’ says about how baptism relates to union with Christ. Roman Catholic teaching (the Council of Trent, Session 5 on original sin and Session 7 on baptism) and the Orthodox churches hold that God unites the person to Christ and washes away sin through the rite itself; Luther's Small Catechism (1529) cites Romans 6:4 to explain what baptism signifies, the daily drowning of the old Adam, while holding that baptism works forgiveness. Reformed confessions call baptism a sign and seal of engrafting into Christ (Westminster Confession 28.1), effective by the Spirit to those who receive it in faith. Baptists and many other evangelicals read the verse as describing what baptism pictures and publicly confesses, a union already made by faith; the Baptist scholar G. R. Beasley-Murray, in Baptism in the New Testament (1962), argued that Paul does speak of the water rite here, as the occasion where faith and God's act meet. Some interpreters take the verse to refer to baptism by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13) rather than water.

Paul's argument uses the practice without endorsing or teaching it, and no other text in Scripture supports it. The verse shows how closely early Christians linked baptism with resurrection hope (compare Romans 6:4-5), but it is too uncertain to found any doctrine or rite.

Baptism into Christ is tied to union with him. Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran theology read the verse as baptism effecting that union; Reformed and Baptist traditions read it as baptism signifying and sealing a union received by faith. All agree that for Paul baptism and faith belong together, and that baptism is not a work of the law.

The phrase ‘blood of the covenant’ links Sinai to the Lord's Supper, where Jesus spoke of the cup as the new covenant in his blood. Christian traditions differ on how Christ is present in the Supper, but all read it as the covenant meal of the new covenant.

Christians disagree on how the Lord's Supper relates to Christ's sacrifice, as the Trent and Reformation debate shows, but all historic traditions affirm that the cross itself is unrepeatable and sufficient.

The pairing of hearts sprinkled and bodies washed joins inner cleansing to baptism, as Titus 3:5 and 1 Peter 3:21 do. Traditions differ on how baptism and inner cleansing are related, but the verse holds them together as the believer's entry into priestly access.
